 6 weather alerts in effect October storms in Arizona can turn severe; here’s why 
 Arizona’s Family First Alert Weather team is tracking an active Wednesday 
 The Arizona’s Family First Alert Weather team is closely monitoring the setup heading into Wednesday. Austin Walker reports on the stormy expectations. By Austin Walker Published : Oct. 20, 2026 at 9:31 PM MST | Updated : 1 hour ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google PHOENIX (AZFamily) — As Arizona heads into what many consider a quiet and calm October, history shows fall storms can be just as aggressive as monsoon storms.
 Last year’s microburst in Tempe is a prime example. The storm knocked out power for tens of thousands of people, damaged more than 1,000 structures and destroyed about 140 homes.
 It’s one reason the Arizona’s Family First Alert Weather team is closely monitoring the setup heading into Wednesday after months of heavy monsoon rain, thunderstorms, flash flooding and powerful wind.
 “We have a crazy setup for October, and when we get October weather patterns like this, we have the potential to see a lot of rain, severe weather, flash flooding, that kind of thing,” First Alert Chief Meteorologist Royal Norman said.
 Norman and the First Alert team are expecting an active Wednesday, fueled by lingering tropical moisture colliding with a system from the Pacific Northwest.
 “Ton of Pacific hurricanes this year, and they keep developing, and so more moisture keeps headed our way. That mixed with the storm system from the Pacific Northwest, and that’s what we got going,” Norman said.
 Norman said it’s a familiar setup — almost identical to last year when the microburst hit Tempe.
 That microburst left businesses closed for weeks, destroyed homes and left families searching for solutions.
 Kayla Vasquez and her mother, Sylvia, live in Chaparral Village off Baseline Road in Tempe, a trailer park hit hard by last year’s storm. The area looks unrecognizable now, but Sylvia said she still panics every time it rains.
 Sylvia said she plans to leave her trailer Wednesday and stay somewhere else because she knows high winds can do serious damage to her home.
 Tornadoes possible?
 Social media is buzzing after the Storm Prediction Center of the National Weather Service forecast a slight risk for tornadoes in parts of the state. Norman said it may feel unusual, but October has produced strange weather before.
 “It’s almost the exact same setup when we had the great hailstorm of 2010 in October, and it’s almost the same setup as when we had the tornado outbreak in Flagstaff of 2010 in October,” Norman said.
 But Norman said not to focus too much on the tornado threat — the bigger concern is heavy rain.
 “We are concerned there could be microbursts. We are concerned [about] flash flooding,” he said. “We’re not predicting it for any one area. We had the microburst in Tempe. We had the huge flood last year in Globe-Miami. We’re not forecasting it for any individual area, but heads-up.”
 The First Alert team will be tracking the storms as they develop and move into the Valley. Meteorologists stress preparation is key.
